# Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification

Masnun Nuha Chowdhury^(†)    Nusrat Jahan Beg^(†)    Umme Hunny Khan
Affiliation: Syed Rifat Raiyan^(‡)    Md Kamrul Hasan    Hasan Mahmud
Affiliation: Systems and Software Lab (SSL), Department of Computer
Science and Engineering Affiliation: Islamic University of Technology,
Dhaka, Bangladesh Affiliation: {masnunnuha, nusratjahan21, ummehunny,
rifatraiyan, hasank, hasan}@iut-dhaka.edu Affiliation: ^(†)Equal
contribution  ^(‡)Corresponding author

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable for high-stakes claim
verification due to hallucinations and shallow reasoning. While
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multi-agent debate (MAD)
address this, they are limited by one-pass retrieval and unstructured
debate dynamics. We propose a courtroom-style multi-agent framework,
PROClaim, that reformulates verification as a structured, adversarial
deliberation. Our approach integrates specialized roles (e.g.,
Plaintiff, Defense, Judge) with Progressive RAG (P-RAG) to dynamically
expand and refine the evidence pool during the debate. Furthermore, we
employ evidence negotiation, self-reflection, and heterogeneous
multi-judge aggregation to enforce calibration, robustness, and
diversity. In zero-shot evaluations on the Check-COVID benchmark,
PROClaim achieves 81.7% accuracy, outperforming standard multi-agent
debate by 10.0 percentage points, with P-RAG driving the primary
performance gains (+7.5 pp). We show that the majority of this
improvement stems from P-RAG’s dynamic coupling of retrieval to the
evolving debate, rather than from any single component in isolation; the
remaining courtroom mechanisms serve to stabilize and de-bias this
process, together providing a robust foundation for reliable claim
verification.

## 1 Introduction

LLMs have demonstrated strong zero-shot performance on
reasoning-intensive tasks, yet their reliability in high-stakes domains,
such as claim verification, remains limited. Despite fluent generation,
LLMs frequently exhibit hallucinations, shallow reasoning, and
overconfident predictions when evaluating evidence-dependent claims
([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)). RAG partially addresses these issues
by grounding responses in external corpora ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib2)). Still, standard pipelines rely on static, single-pass
retrieval ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)) and lack mechanisms for
iterative reasoning, often resulting in incomplete or biased
conclusions.

To improve reliability, recent work has explored Multi-Agent Debate
(MAD), where multiple LLM instances iteratively argue and refine answers
([Du et al., 2024](#bib.bib11); [Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Han et
al., 2025](#bib.bib3)). While promising, prior studies show that
unstructured debate often leads to premature convergence, shared bias
reinforcement, and limited evidence exploration ([Smit et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)). In particular, agent
agreement is frequently misinterpreted as correctness, even when
grounded in insufficient or biased evidence.

In this work, we propose PROClaim (Progressive Retrieval Orchestrated
multi-agent framework for Claim verification), centered on Progressive
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (P-RAG), an iterative, query-adaptive
retrieval mechanism that continuously expands and refines the evidence
pool as debate unfolds. To generate the structured, evolving
deliberation that P-RAG draws on for retrieval, we adopt a
courtroom-style multi-agent framework that reformulates claim
verification as a structured, adversarial reasoning process. Inspired by
legal systems and recent agent-based simulations ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib18)), this includes explicit roles (Plaintiff, Defense,
Judge, Critic, and Expert Witness), evidence admission protocols, and
multi-stage deliberation.  
Contributions. We present a unified framework where structured
deliberation outperforms standard multi-agent debate, achieving a +10.0
pp accuracy gain and validating a courtroom-style architecture. Dynamic
retrieval via P-RAG is the primary driver, adding 7.5 points while
preventing evidence stagnation. We further show that model diversity is
crucial: heterogeneous LLMs exhibit complementary errors that offset
each other, outperforming any single model. PROClaim also demonstrates
strong zero-shot, domain-agnostic performance. Beyond gains, our
analysis reveals deeper insights into multi-agent reasoning:

- $`\bullet`$
  Breaking the epistemic bubble, removing dynamic retrieval (P-RAG)
  increases inter-judge agreement
  ($`\bar{\kappa}=0.468\rightarrow 0.599`$) while reducing accuracy by
  7.5 pp, revealing confident convergence on incorrect conclusions.
- $`\bullet`$
  Acting as a logic-level lie detector, incorrect predictions exhibit
  unstable reasoning trajectories with oscillating self-reflection
  scores, showing that reasoning dynamics are more informative than
  final confidence.
- $`\bullet`$
  Heterogeneous judges exhibit complementary error profiles (e.g.,
  over-refutation vs. cautious abstention), whose combination yields a
  3.3 pp accuracy gain over single-judge panels.
- $`\bullet`$
  Serving as an economic governor, removing self-reflection increases
  debate rounds by 29% (5.47 $`\rightarrow`$ 7.06) and token usage by
  17% (210.9K $`\rightarrow`$ 247.3K), while changing accuracy by only
  0.8 pp.
- $`\bullet`$
  Demonstrating the butterfly effect of argument framing: small biases
  in premise decomposition propagate to final outcomes, as Run-2 reduces
  $`\kappa_{GT}`$ from 0.423(Run-0) to 0.384 despite stable inter-judge
  $`\kappa`$.
- $`\bullet`$
  Revealing structural negativity bias: LLM judges overproduce Refute
  relative to ground truth and converge faster on such claims (0.2
  primary and 0.3 role-switched rounds), indicating training-induced
  conservatism.

Together, these findings reframe LLM reasoning as a dynamic process,
where reliability arises from the structure, diversity, and evolution of
deliberation, not just final answers. We provide our code and data in
the following GitHub repository:
[https://github.com/mnc13/PROClaim](https://github.com/mnc13/PROClaim).

## 2 Related Work

Retrieval. RAG grounds generation in external corpora ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib2); [Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)), and iterative
variants improve coverage by re-querying from intermediate generations
([Shao et al., 2023](#bib.bib48); [Trivedi et al., 2023](#bib.bib47);
[Park et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). Retrieval nonetheless remains driven
by a single reasoner’s state, leaving it exposed to confirmatory bias
under conflicting evidence ([Ge et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)).

Debate. MAD improves factuality by having agents critique one another
([Du et al., 2024](#bib.bib11); [Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) and has
been adapted to fact-checking ([Han et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Ma et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [He et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)). Controlled
analyses, however, report premature convergence, conformity bias, and
sensitivity to configuration ([Smit et al., 2024](#bib.bib17); [Wu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib28); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)): homogeneous
panels rarely improve on majority vote. Hybrid systems attach retrieval
to debate ([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib25); [Jeong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24); [Li et al., 2025c](#bib.bib26)), but draw from fixed
or loosely coupled evidence pools.

Structure and coordination. Courtroom simulations show that explicit
roles stabilise high-stakes deliberation ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib18); [Chun et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib51)), while role assignment ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)), role switching ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)),
self-reflection ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib4); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib49)), dedicated critics ([Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50)),
and multi-model juries ([Verga et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)) each address
one failure mode in isolation.

PROClaim couples them: retrieval queries are compiled from the live
debate state and reflection gaps rather than issued once upfront,
role-switching is repurposed from bias mitigation into a consistency
diagnostic, judges evaluate the deliberative trajectory rather than a
final answer, and termination is governed by epistemic signals. Each
ingredient exists somewhere; the closed loop, and the failure modes it
measurably prevents, are the contribution.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Related Work: Additional Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
expands this discussion.

## 3 Methodology

We propose a courtroom-inspired pipeline for zero-shot,
evidence-grounded fact-checking of COVID-19-related claims. Each claim
is treated as a legal case: a _Plaintiff Counsel_ supports it, a
_Defense Counsel_ challenges it, and an independent judicial panel
delivers the verdict, imposing disciplined adversarial structure over
the reasoning process.
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
provides a high-level overview, with the full evaluation cycle detailed
in
Appendix [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Pseudo-code ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

![Refer to caption](2603.28488v3/figg.png)

Figure 1: Overview of the courtroom-style claim-verification pipeline in
PROClaim.

### 3.1 Argument Mining

Before retrieval, the raw claim is decomposed into atomic, independently
testable _premises_ ([Hu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib41); [Lawrence and Reed,
2017](#bib.bib42)). Given a claim $`c`$, the miner produces
$`\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{k}\}`$, where each $`p_{i}`$ is a single
verifiable proposition and the adaptive size $`k`$ captures the claim’s
non-redundant semantic content. These premises guide targeted retrieval
and provide an explicit checklist for evaluating argument completeness
during self-reflection and critic assessment
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Self-Reflection and Critic Evaluation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

### 3.2 Evidence Retrieval and Selection

Relevant evidence is retrieved from a study-specific corpus of
approximately 360,000 COVID-19 PubMed abstracts (2020–2024) using the
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 bi-encoder ([Gao and Callan, 2021](#bib.bib43);
[Reimers and Gurevych, 2019](#bib.bib39)). A FAISS index ([Douze et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)) is queried once per premise
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Argument Mining ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"))
to form an initial shared pool while retaining publication and
provenance metadata. Stance-conditioned supporting and opposing queries
mitigate the bias of static Top-$`k`$ retrieval under conflicting
evidence ([Wu and Saxena, 2025](#bib.bib44)); the resulting pools are
exchanged before debate so each counsel can refine its case against the
opposing evidence. Each retrieved document is assigned an admissibility
score

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       w=r\times c,
       ```           |     |

where $`r,c\in[0,1]`$ denote relevance and credibility, respectively.
Evidence with $`w>0.5`$ is admitted, $`0.1<w\leq 0.5`$ is marked as
disputed, and the remainder is discarded. The admitted evidence is
ranked by $`w`$ and passed to the debate stage
(Appendix [G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 Admissibility Scoring Prompt ‣ Appendix G Prompt Templates ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

Our admissibility criterion follows the observation that evidence
quality and provenance are as important as relevance when resolving
conflicting claims ([Ge et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)). Accordingly, we
score each candidate jointly on relevance and credibility, inspired by
the Daubert Standard ([Legal Information Institute, 2024](#bib.bib38)),
which emphasizes the admissibility of reliable scientific evidence.

### 3.3 Progressive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (P-RAG)

Static, one-time retrieval is ill-suited to adversarial debate as new
evidential gaps emerge as arguments evolve. Unlike prior iterative
approaches that query solely from the previous generation ([Shao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib48); [Trivedi et al., 2023](#bib.bib47)), P-RAG
concatenates three sources: (i) the last four messages of the rolling
debate context (a bounded recency window), (ii) the agent’s
self-identified evidential gap, and (iii) reflection-driven discovery
needs from the prior round
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Self-Reflection and Critic Evaluation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")),
into one prompt with the Judge refining each query before execution (see
App. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 P-RAG Query Construction ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
for full logic and prompts). To prevent redundant retrieval, each
candidate item is scored against the existing pool:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\operatorname{novelty}(d)=1-\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\cos(e_{d},\,e_{p})
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$ is the current pool and $`e_{\cdot}`$ denotes an
L2-normalised embedding. Unlike global diversity metrics such as the
Vendi Score ([Rezaei and Dieng, 2025](#bib.bib46)), our novelty filter
operates iteratively, rejecting near-duplicates at each round.

Only items with novelty $`\geq 0.20`$ are admitted. This threshold is
not ad hoc: it was selected by grid search over
$`\{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30\}`$ on a held-out development subset;
values below 0.15 allow near-duplicates, while values above 0.30
prematurely discard nuanced but critical evidence. Retrieval terminates
early under the adaptive stopping criteria in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Progressive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (P-RAG) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

| Criterion        |  Threshold  |  Rationale                |
|------------------|-------------|---------------------------|
| Novelty filter   |  $`<0.20`$  |  Rejects near-duplicates  |
| Redundancy ratio |  $`>70\%`$  |  Indicates saturation     |
| Relevance gain   |  $`<0.05`$  |  Diminishing returns      |
| Iteration cap    |  $`10`$     |  Limits compute cost      |

Table 1: P-RAG stopping criteria.

### 3.4 Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) Orchestration

The multi-agent debate is the central reasoning engine of the framework,
comprising five adjudication roles: Plaintiff Counsel, Defense Counsel,
and three Judges. Each role is instantiated with an LLM appropriate for
its function
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.4 Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) Orchestration ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"));
these assignments are illustrative rather than prescriptive, and the
framework is compatible with alternative models. Controlled evidence
indicates that homogeneous agents cannot reliably improve over majority
voting ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)). We therefore introduce model
heterogeneity across advocacy, critique, expert testimony, and
adjudication; this complements dynamic role-assignment
approaches ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) while promoting diverse
reasoning and reducing correlated errors.

| Role | Model | Prov. | T. |
|----|----|----|----|
| Premise Decomp. |  deepseek-r1 | OR | 0.7 |
| Plaintiff Counsel |  gpt-5-mini | OA | 0.5 |
| Defense Counsel |  deepseek-v3.2 | OR | 0.5 |
| The Court | ![\[Uncaptioned image\]](2603.28488v3/qwen.png) qwen3-235b-a22b | OR | 0.2 |
| Expert Witness |  hermes-3-llama-405b | OR | 0.5 |
| Critic Agent |  deepseek-r1 | OR | 0.3 |
| Consistency Anal. |  deepseek-v3.2 | OR | 0.3 |
| Judge 1 |  deepseek-r1 | OR | 0.3 |
| Judge 2 |  hermes-3-llama-405b | OR | 0.3 |
| Judge 3 | ![\[Uncaptioned image\]](2603.28488v3/qwen.png) qwen3-235b-a22b | OR | 0.3 |

Table 2: Role-wise models. Providers (Prov.): OR=OpenRouter, OA=OpenAI.
T.=Temperature.

Each round consists of five stages: (1) Evidence discovery, where both
agents identify evidential gaps and retrieve additional evidence via
P-RAG; (2) Argument generation, producing evidence-grounded arguments;
(3) Expert testimony, where the Judge may invoke a dynamically
instantiated domain expert when needed; (4) Self-reflection, whose
identified gaps are injected into the next P-RAG query
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Self-Reflection and Critic Evaluation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"));
and (5) Critic evaluation, where an independent Critic assesses both
arguments and may trigger early termination.

The debate runs for at most 10 rounds and terminates early if any of the
following conditions are met: (i) reflection plateau
($`|\Delta\,\texttt{total\_reflection\_score}|<0.05`$ for two
consecutive rounds), (ii) critic resolution (debate_resolved=True),
(iii) novelty exhaustion (average novelty $`<0.10`$ across two
consecutive P-RAG calls), or (iv) judicial signal indicating readiness
for deliberation.

### 3.5 Self-Reflection and Critic Evaluation

Per-agent self-reflection. After each round, each counsel performs
structured self-reflection ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib4); [Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib49)) along three dimensions: *logic* ($`l`$),
*novelty* ($`n`$), and *rebuttal* ($`b`$), each in $`[0,1]`$. Their
relative weights (0.4, 0.3, 0.3) were determined *a priori* through a
structured expert elicitation following the SHELF/Delphi protocol
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Expert Elicitation of Self-Reflection Weights ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
The reflection score is computed as

|     |                                      |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\text{ref}}=0.4\,l+0.3\,n+0.3\,b,
       ```                                   |     | (2) |

and converted into a confidence adjustment,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{\text{ref}}=(s_{\text{ref}}-0.5)\times 0.6\in[-0.30,\,+0.30],
``` |  | (3) |

The $`0.6`$ multiplier limits the adjustment to $`\pm 0.30`$, allowing
self-reflection to refine without overriding the panel’s baseline
confidence ($`c_{\text{base}}\approx 0.8`$). The reflection output also
identifies missing evidence for the subsequent P-RAG retrieval query.

Independent Critic Agent. An independent Critic Agent evaluates each
round, motivated by prior work showing dedicated critics outperform
self-critique ([Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50)). It scores both arguments
on logic, evidence coverage, and rebuttal, identifies unresolved
premises
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Argument Mining ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")),
provides feedback, and issues the debate_resolved signal.

### 3.6 Role-Switching Consistency Test

We introduce a role-switching consistency test to distinguish
evidence-grounded reasoning from position anchoring. Unlike prior work
using role-switching for bias reduction or uncertainty estimation ([Jin
et al., 2025](#bib.bib51); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)), we use it
diagnostically. After the primary debate, the counsels swap roles, the
state is reset, and the debate is repeated. A separate LLM compares both
transcripts for contradictions and selective evidence use, producing an
agent-level *consistency score* for final confidence weighting
(Section [3.7](#S3.SS7 "3.7 Judicial Panel Evaluation and Final Verdict ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

### 3.7 Judicial Panel Evaluation and Final Verdict

The complete case record, including both debate transcripts, admitted
evidence, P-RAG histories, critic evaluations, and self-reflection
scores, is submitted to three independent LLM judges using different
models to reduce correlated errors ([Verga et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)).
Each judge evaluates case reconstruction, evidence strength, argument
validity, source reliability, and retrieval rigour before assigning one
of three verdicts: Supported, Not Supported, or Inconclusive. The final
verdict is determined by majority vote
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Consensus Edge-Cases ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

Base confidence:

|     |                                     |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       c_{\text{base}}=0.8\,\sigma+0.3\,q,
       ```                                  |     | (4) |

where $`\sigma=\texttt{winning\_votes}/\texttt{total\_votes}`$
represents consensus strength and
$`q=(\bar{s}_{\text{ev}}+\bar{s}_{\text{val}}+\bar{s}_{\text{rel}})/30`$
is the normalized mean score for evidence, validity, and reliability.
The consensus weight was selected through 5-fold cross-validated grid
search to minimize Expected Calibration Error ([Gu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)). The final configuration achieved an ECE of
$`0.034`$, compared with $`0.18`$ for standard averaging
(Appendix [C.2.1](#A3.SS2.SSS1 "C.2.1 Confidence Calibration Analysis ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification");
weight details in
Appendix [C.2.2](#A3.SS2.SSS2 "C.2.2 Confidence Aggregation and the Certainty Buffer ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

Adjustment:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{\text{final}}=\text{clamp}\bigl(c_{\text{base}}+\delta_{\text{rs}}+\delta_{\text{ref}},\;0,\;1\bigr),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\delta_{\text{rs}}`$ is the role-switch adjustment and
$`\delta_{\text{ref}}`$ is the winning side’s final reflection
adjustment. The latter is lower-bounded at $`-0.15`$ to prevent
self-critique from overriding the judicial consensus. When at least two
judges agree, the final confidence is also lower-bounded at $`0.10`$
(Appendices [C.2.3](#A3.SS2.SSS3 "C.2.3 Role-Switch Consistency Mapping (𝛿_"rs") ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
and
[C.2.4](#A3.SS2.SSS4 "C.2.4 Self-Reflection Asymmetric Bounding (𝛿_"ref") ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

## 4 Experimental Setup

Dataset. To evaluate the framework’s capacity for adversarial
resolution, we focus on the subset of the Check-COVID ([Wang et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib35)) test set possessing definitive binary ground-truths
(SUPPORT or REFUTE), comprising 120 claims evaluated across three
independent runs (360 debate instances).

Retrieval Corpus. Retrieval is performed over a static corpus of
COVID-19 abstracts from PubMed (2020–2024), constructed for this study.
Source metadata, including PMID, title, journal, and publication year,
are stored alongside each passage to support provenance tracking.

Configuration and Metrics.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.4 Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) Orchestration ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
summarizes the LLM assignment, where agent roles are partitioned across
distinct architectures based on their functional capacity (deliberative
vs. evaluative) and cognitive profile, utilizing moderate temperatures
for adversarial advocacy and lower temperatures for rigorous judicial
evaluation (details in
Appendix [B.1.3](#A2.SS1.SSS3 "B.1.3 Agent Configurations ‣ B.1 Reproducibility ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
PROClaim is model-agnostic by design; the reported configuration is one
instantiation. Key retrieval hyperparameters are a novelty threshold
$`\tau{=}0.20`$, per-round top-$`k{=}3`$, and admissibility floor
$`w{>}0.5`$; full settings are in
Appendix [B.1.4](#A2.SS1.SSS4 "B.1.4 Hyperparameters ‣ B.1 Reproducibility ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

We evaluate classification performance (accuracy, macro F1), inter-judge
reliability (Cohen’s $`\kappa`$, unanimity/split rates), and efficiency
(token usage, debate rounds, evidence pool size).

## 5 Results and Discussion

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
reports Check-COVID performance across three independent runs, with
aggregate results obtained via majority voting. Our framework adopts an
adversarial *Burden of Refutation*: if a claim withstands deliberation
and the judicial panel cannot reach a definitive Refute verdict,
returning Inconclusive due to insufficient opposing evidence, it is
classified as Supported. This evaluation protocol follows the courtroom
principle that claims are upheld unless successfully refuted
(Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 The ‘Burden of Refutation’ Standard ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

| Run       | Acc   | m-F1  | $`\bar{\kappa}`$ | Agr.  | Unan. | Split |
|-----------|-------|-------|------------------|-------|-------|-------|
| Run-0     | 0.950 | 0.950 | 0.429            | 0.617 | 0.442 | 0.558 |
| Run-1     | 0.817 | 0.817 | 0.549            | 0.700 | 0.558 | 0.442 |
| Run-2     | 0.790 | 0.790 | 0.474            | 0.652 | 0.496 | 0.504 |
| W. Total  | 0.841 | 0.841 | 0.484            | 0.656 | 0.499 | 0.501 |

### 5.1 Main Pipeline Performance

Majority voting achieves 81.7% accuracy, while the 95.8% oracle ceiling
bounds performance under favourable initialization. Inter-judge
agreement remains stable across runs ($`\kappa`$: 0.429, 0.549, 0.474)
despite expected variance in cascaded LLM pipelines ([Atıl et al.,
2025](#bib.bib57)), which PROClaim’s audit trail makes interpretable.
Run-1 retains 0.817 accuracy despite lower ground-truth agreement
($`\kappa_{GT}=0.372`$) through balanced errors. In Run-2, biased
premise decomposition suppresses Refute recall and lowers
$`\kappa_{GT}`$ to 0.384 while inter-judge $`\kappa`$ remains 0.474,
indicating systematic bias rather than structural failure.

### 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(a) Debate termination reasons.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(b) Rounds to consensus by ground-truth label.

Figure 2: Termination distribution and convergence speed across 360
debate instances.

(a) Novelty decay across rounds.

(b) Novelty distribution by round.

Figure 3: P-RAG evidence novelty across debate rounds.

Figure 4: Reflection score trajectories across plateau, judicial, and
critic resolution patterns.

Termination distribution:
Figure [2(a)](#S5.F2.sf1 "In Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
shows that most debates self-terminate through reflection-driven
signals: Reflection Plateau and Judicial Signal. Reflection Plateau
enforces adaptive halting once marginal argumentative gains diminish,
mitigating circular reasoning. The low incidence of Novelty
Stabilization (3.1%) further suggests that termination is driven by
argumentative saturation rather than corpus insufficiency.

Convergence speed:
Figure [2(b)](#S5.F2.sf2 "In Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
shows that REFUTE claims converge faster than SUPPORT claims in both the
primary (0.2 rounds faster) and role-switched debates (0.3 rounds
faster), consistent with the LLM negativity bias documented in
Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Judicial Panel: Reliability and Negativity Bias ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

Evidence novelty decay:
Figures [3(a)](#S5.F3.sf1 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")–[3(b)](#S5.F3.sf2 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
confirm that P-RAG sustains genuine evidential discovery across all
active rounds, with query novelty approaching the threshold from round 4
onward. The narrowing violin distributions from round 3 indicate pool
saturation, empirically validating the 0.20 novelty threshold as the
natural boundary between productive and redundant retrieval, justifying
the adaptive stopping design.

Reflection trajectories:
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Debate Dynamics and Adaptive Stopping ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
plots per-claim self-reflection score trajectories across debate rounds
$`t`$: each line corresponds to one claim-level debate ($`\sim`$10
representative claims sampled per panel across runs), and each panel
stratifies debates by their termination condition. The stratification
reveals distinct convergence behaviours: Reflection Plateau yields rapid
stabilisation within 3–4 rounds, Judicial Signal extends deliberation
for contested claims, and Critic Resolution exhibits higher variance.
Across all conditions, incorrect predictions display greater inter-round
oscillation whereas correct predictions converge smoothly, a behavioural
signature of erroneous outcomes that single-pass pipelines cannot
expose.

### 5.3 Comparison with Baselines

| System                          | Acc    | MacroF1 | Ev   |
|---------------------------------|--------|---------|------|
| Single-call DeepSeek-v3.2 + RAG | 0.8000 | 0.7972  | 18.5 |
| Standard MAD                    | 0.7167 | 0.7068  | 12.1 |
| PROClaim (Majority Vote)        | 0.8167 | 0.8165  | 67.5 |

Table 4: PROClaim vs. baselines on Check-COVID. Ev denotes average
evidence pool size per claim.

Against two-agent, single-judge Standard MAD (71.7%), PROClaim’s gain is
significant on HealthVer (McNemar’s $`\chi^{2}=8.04`$, $`p=0.0046`$,
odds ratio 3.67;
Section [5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Cross-Domain Generalization and Paired Baseline Comparison ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

Single-call RAG is competitive in-domain (80.0%) but framing-sensitive:
identical evidence supports opposing arguments in our role-switch case
study
([subsection F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Role-Switching Case Study ‣ Appendix F Qualitative Case Study ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
On HealthVer it falls to 63.0%, while PROClaim declines from 81.7% to
72.0%, widening the gap from 1.7 to 9.0 pp
(Section [5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Cross-Domain Generalization and Paired Baseline Comparison ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
Single-agent iterative RAG would confound retrieval policy with
architecture; our controlled comparison is the w/o-P-RAG ablation
($`-7.5`$ pp,
Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

Beyond accuracy, PROClaim prioritizes Deliberative Traceability:
variance in judge scores and agent consistency surfaces a Trajectory
Instability Signal, a “Logic Lie Detector” for contested claims
inherently absent in single-call black-box pipelines (artifact inventory
in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Deliberative Traceability: Artifact Inventory ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")),
and its confidence is nearly perfectly calibrated (ECE $`=0.034`$ vs.
0.18 under naive aggregation;
Appendix [C.2.1](#A3.SS2.SSS1 "C.2.1 Confidence Calibration Analysis ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
The 95.8% Oracle ceiling further establishes that the architecture’s
attainable bound exceeds every reported baseline.

Table 6: Ablation results on 120 claims. $`\Delta`$Acc is measured
relative to the full PROClaim pipeline. Ev denotes the average evidence
pool size per claim. Each round count reflects the sum of primary and
role-switched debate rounds per claim.

P-RAG is the most impactful component ($`\downarrow 7.5`$ pp): without
it, the evidence pool nearly halves (37.5 vs. 67.5), debates run longer
(6.00 vs. 5.47) on weaker evidence, and inter-judge agreement rises to
$`\kappa=0.599`$, a *negative* signal of convergence without correctness
(*epistemic bubble*). Role-switching contributes $`-4.2`$ pp and reduces
the evidence pool by 20%, confirming the second pass surfaces missed
evidence rather than serving as a mere consistency check. A single judge
costs 3.3 pp, directly quantifying the benefit of heterogeneous
adjudication
(Sec. [3.7](#S3.SS7 "3.7 Judicial Panel Evaluation and Final Verdict ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
Self-reflection has minimal accuracy impact ($`-0.8`$ pp) but drives
efficiency: removing it increases rounds by 29% (5.47 $`\rightarrow`$
7.06) and token usage by 17% (210.9K $`\rightarrow`$ 247.3K), confirming
that its early-stopping signal makes the pipeline cost-effective. A full
token usage breakdown and analysis are provided in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Computational Cost and Scalability Analysis ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

### 5.5 Judicial Panel: Reliability and Negativity Bias

Inter-judge agreement ($`\kappa_{\text{mean}}=0.468`$; 48.9% unanimous)
shows that the heterogeneous panel disagrees in 51.1% of cases.
DeepSeek-R1 *aggressively refutes* (high Refute recall but false-refutes
Support), Hermes-3-405B *cautiously abstains* (frequent Inconclusive on
Support), and Qwen3-235B-A22B remains the *most calibrated* (highest
Support recall and balanced abstention). Although all overproduce Refute
or Inconclusive, indicating structural negativity bias, their distinct
commission, omission, and calibration errors allow disagreement to
correct rather than compound mistakes. Accordingly, majority voting
achieves balanced judge–ground-truth agreement
($`\kappa_{\text{GT}}\in[0.431,0.468]`$, mean $`0.450`$), supporting
heterogeneous voting as a means of improving reliability.

HealthVer. On a uniformly sampled set of 100 claims, the framework

Using a Wikipedia-based retriever, it achieves 78.3% accuracy on 60
sampled claims, within $`\sim`$3 pp of Check-COVID ([Aly et al.,

These proof-of-concept robustness checks use sampled subsets because
full-corpus deliberation requires approximately 211K tokens per claim.
With zero domain-specific tuning and only the retrieval backend changed,

generality of the deliberative architecture

pp: parametric shortcuts do not generalize; the deliberative
architecture’s gains persist.

### 5.7 Sycophancy and Argument Integrity

Sycophancy, the tendency of agents to yield to opposing arguments
([Malmqvist, 2025](#bib.bib54)), is low overall: role-play consistency
(Plaintiff 7.80/10; Defense 6.22/10) shows only mild asymmetry from
Defense “leaking” prior-role reasoning after switches; concession rates
are minimal (0.03 / 0.01 per 1,000 words), the higher Plaintiff rate
consistent with the negativity bias
(Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Judicial Panel: Reliability and Negativity Bias ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"));
the reflection plateau averages 0.3823 per round, far above the 0.05
stagnation threshold, confirming agents push novel reasoning rather than
colluding; and judicial conformity (Fleiss’ $`\kappa=0.4513`$) affirms
independent evaluation while precluding the absolute conformity
($`\kappa\to 1.0`$) symptomatic of systemic sycophancy
(Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Sycophancy and Argument Integrity Metrics ‣ Appendix E Additional Quantitative Results ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

## 6 Conclusion

PROClaim shows that courtroom-style deliberation yields a
claim-verification system that is accurate, calibrated, and auditable.
By closing the loop between debate and retrieval, and policing it with
procedural safeguards borrowed from legal practice, we establish that
reliability in multi-agent LLM systems emerges from deliberative
architecture rather than individual model capability, offering a
principled, empirically validated template for high-stakes verification.
Future work includes live PubMed retrieval, extension to other
high-stakes domains, and token reduction via early-exit and
distillation.

## Limitations

Computational cost. Full deliberation consumes $`\sim`$211K tokens per
claim, roughly $`11\times`$ Standard MAD. Our ablations show each costly
component buys measurable accuracy;
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Computational Cost and Scalability Analysis ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
maps the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier with reduction pathways for
latency-sensitive settings.

Run-level variance. Identically configured runs vary (0.790–0.950
accuracy), consistent with non-determinism in cascaded LLM pipelines
([Atıl et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). Our audit record makes this
interpretable
(Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Main Pipeline Performance ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"));
majority voting bounds but does not eliminate it.

Rationale faithfulness. The structured case record (evidence with
provenance, transcripts, reflection/consistency scores) is computed
programmatically and auditable; judges’ *verbal* rationales, however,
inherit the open problem that LLM chains-of-thought need not reflect
underlying computation ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib58)). PROClaim thus
offers *deliberative traceability*, complementary to and weaker than the
formal verifiability of argumentation-theoretic frameworks ([Freedman et
al., 2025](#bib.bib59)); we do not claim faithful explanation.

Evaluation scale and instantiation. Cross-domain results use sampled
subsets (100 HealthVer / 60 FEVEROUS, full-corpus deliberation being
cost-prohibitive) and are proof-of-concept checks with paired
significance testing. The reported role assignment is one
budget-constrained instantiation of a model-agnostic design; validating
alternatives, e.g. open-weight panels, is left to future work.

## Ethics Statement

PROClaim is designed to *support* evidence-grounded verification of
controversial, evidence-dependent claims, a defensive application of
LLMs against misinformation. All experiments use publicly available
benchmarks (Check-COVID, HealthVer, FEVEROUS) and published PubMed
abstracts; no personal data is processed. The system’s verdicts are
research outputs and must not be used as a substitute for professional
medical judgment; for any deployment touching health decisions we
prescribe the conservative verdict mapping and human-in-the-loop review.
The full audit trail the framework produces is intended precisely to
keep human overseers able to contest and correct its conclusions.

## Appendix A Related Work: Additional Details

Retrieval-Augmented Generation. RAG enhances factual grounding in large
language models by incorporating external knowledge at inference time
([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib2); [Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)).
Recent work improves retrieval quality through structured pipelines such
as coarse-to-fine retrieval ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) and
retrieval with reasoning ([Park et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)), helping
mitigate hallucinations ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)). Hybrid
approaches further embed retrieval into multi-agent and iterative
reasoning systems, including debate-augmented RAG ([Hu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib25)), Tool-MAD ([Jeong et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)),
R-Debater ([Li et al., 2025c](#bib.bib26)), CircuitLM ([Hasan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib5)), and multi-source retrieval frameworks ([Gong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)), underscoring the need for adaptive evidence
acquisition under conflicting or noisy conditions ([Ge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45)). However, most approaches rely on pre-collected
evidence pools or limited iterative mechanisms, lacking retrieval
continuously driven by structured deliberation. Recent work also shows
that claim decomposition’s benefits in fact-checking depend on how
sub-claims are constructed ([Hu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib41)), motivating
its reuse as a means of extracting premise-level units to guide targeted
retrieval.

Multi-Agent Debate. MAD has emerged as an effective paradigm for
improving reasoning, factuality, and robustness in LLM outputs ([Du et
al., 2024](#bib.bib11)), with variants spanning group-based discussions
([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)), efficiency-oriented architectures
([Fan et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), and fact-checking frameworks ([Han et
al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [He et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)). Extensions incorporating credibility scoring and
evidence aggregation further improve performance in high-stakes
verification tasks ([Dong and Ito, 2026](#bib.bib31); [Li et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib23); [Rahman et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)). By enabling
agents to critique and refine each other’s reasoning, debate reduces
hallucinations and improves consensus quality. However, controlled
analyses reveal persistent limitations including premature convergence,
conformity bias, and sensitivity to agent configuration ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib30); [Smit et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), motivating more structured debate protocols.

Agent Coordination and Learning Dynamics. To address these limitations,
recent work explores improved coordination mechanisms in multi-agent
systems, including dynamic role assignment ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)), uncertainty-aware role switching ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22)), and self-reflection frameworks such as Self-Refine
([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib4)) and MAR ([Ozer et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Siddique et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). Diversity and
reasoning coverage are further improved through persona-based debate
([Hu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib29); [Hu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib1)) and
divergent thinking strategies ([Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)), while
knowledge-enhanced and tool-augmented systems incorporate external
signals to strengthen reasoning ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Jeong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)). Despite these advances, existing methods
treat these components as independent objectives, whereas PROClaim
repurposes them within a unified pipeline, where role-switching serves
as a consistency diagnostic and self-reflection actively drives
subsequent evidence retrieval.

Structured Deliberation and Courtroom Simulation. Structured debate
frameworks introduce stronger inductive biases to stabilize multi-agent
reasoning. Courtroom-style simulations such as AgentCourt ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib18)) and AgenticSimLaw ([Chun et al., 2026](#bib.bib7))
demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit roles and adversarial
interaction in high-stakes decision-making, while recent systems combine
debate with retrieval for multi-round verification ([Wang et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib20); [Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib25)). While these
approaches improve robustness, they typically lack tightly integrated,
dynamic retrieval mechanisms that evolve alongside the debate process,
limiting their applicability to open-domain fact verification.

Debate-Based Evaluation and Argumentation-Theoretic Verification. A
parallel line of work employs adversarial debate for *LLM output
evaluation* rather than claim verification. D3 ([Harrasse et al.,
2026](#bib.bib60)) uses courtroom-style debate to rank pairs of
candidate responses cost-effectively, but the setting is closed-book by
construction: no corpus, retrieval, or external evidence is involved.
PROClaim’s debate instead *constructs* an evidence record over a
360K-document corpus, with retrieval, admissibility, and provenance as
first-class citizens, targeting verification rather than pairwise
comparison of generations. Separately, argumentation-theoretic systems
such as ArgLLMs ([Freedman et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)) construct
quantitative bipolar argumentation graphs whose verdicts are *formally
faithful* to the argument structure by mathematical construction, a
strong guarantee obtained by operating on retrieval-free, QA-derived
claims. PROClaim targets the complementary regime of evidence-dependent
controversial claims requiring dynamic corpus exploration, offering
*deliberative traceability* (auditable process records) rather than
formal entailment guarantees; the two notions of explainability are
distinguished explicitly in our Limitations.

Overall, prior work largely treats retrieval, debate, and coordination
as separate or loosely coupled components: retrieval as preprocessing,
debate as answer refinement, judging as one-shot scoring. PROClaim
advances this line of research by closing the loop among them: retrieval
queries are compiled from the live debate state and reflection gaps,
role-switching is repurposed from a bias-mitigation trick into a
consistency diagnostic, judges evaluate the full deliberative trajectory
rather than a final answer, and termination is governed by epistemic
signals. Each mechanism exists in some form in isolation; their
closed-loop coupling, and the failure modes it measurably prevents
(epistemic bubbles, evidence stagnation, position-anchored
argumentation), are the contribution.

## Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details

### B.1 Reproducibility

We provide the repository containing the full implementation of our
framework, including all configurations, prompts, and evaluation
scripts.

Source Code:
[https://github.com/mnc13/PROClaim](https://github.com/mnc13/PROClaim)

#### B.1.1 Software Environment and Dependencies

All experiments were conducted utilizing Python 3.8+. We isolated our
reasoning engine using external API calls to language models, but local
orchestration relies on a strict set of dependencies. The core local
libraries encompass:

- •
  Deep Learning Framework: PyTorch v1.7.0
- •
  Vector Search Engine: faiss-cpu (configured with IndexFlatIP for
  inner-product cosine similarity searches)
- •
  Text Embedding & Processing: transformers v3.4.0 and
  sentence-transformers
- •
  Numerical Operations: NumPy v1.19.1

#### B.1.2 Data Processing and Corpus Assumptions

Input Dataset. We evaluate our framework on the Check-COVID dataset,
focusing on claims from the test split with definitive labels (SUPPORTED
or REFUTED). Claims are passed to the extraction agents without lexical
normalization or stemming, preserving full linguistic semantics.

Knowledge Corpus External knowledge is provided via a subset of PubMed
abstracts related to COVID-19 (2020–2024). Offline processing embeds
these abstracts into a 1.4 GB FAISS continuous vector index utilizing
the 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model with normalized embeddings.

#### B.1.3 Agent Configurations

Our framework adopts a deliberate separation between argumentative and
evaluative components to ensure reliable adjudication. Adversarial
debate is conducted between heterogeneous models (GPT-5 mini and
DeepSeek-V3.2), introducing diversity in reasoning styles and reducing
the likelihood of homogeneous argument patterns.

Evaluation is performed by a multi-model judicial panel, which includes
DeepSeek-R1 alongside other independent large language models. Final
decisions are determined via majority voting, ensuring that no single
model exerts disproportionate influence over the outcome.

Importantly, we enforce architectural separation between generation and
evaluation stages: models used for advocacy (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2) are
distinct from those used for judgment (e.g., DeepSeek-R1). This design
ensures that argument construction and adjudication are carried out by
systems with differing training paradigms and inference characteristics,
thereby promoting more balanced and independent evaluation.

The exact model mappings and generation sampling temperatures ($`T`$)
defined for each architectural role are as follows:

- •
  Plaintiff Counsel (Proponent): gpt-5-mini ($`T=0.5`$)
- •
  Defense Counsel (Opponent): deepseek-v3.2 ($`T=0.5`$)
- •
  The Court: qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 ($`T=0.2`$)
- •
  Judicial Panel (Final Evaluation): A tripartite system combining
  deepseek-r1, hermes-3-llama-3.1-405b, and qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 (all
  strictly set to $`T=0.3`$ for highly deterministic arbitration).
- •
  Support Agents: Premise decomposition is performed using deepseek-r1
  ($`T=0.7`$). Expert Witnesses are dynamically generated utilizing
  hermes-3-llama-3.1-405b ($`T=0.5`$), while the Critic Agent relies on
  deepseek-r1 ($`T=0.3`$) and the Consistency Analyzer uses
  deepseek-v3.2 ($`T=0.3`$).

Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.1.3 Agent Configurations ‣ B.1 Reproducibility ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
records the functional rationale for each primary assignment. Two
clarifications are in order. First, heterogeneous assignment is the
*principled architectural baseline* for studying debate dynamics, not a
tuned hyperparameter: exhaustively searching model pairings is neither
feasible nor the point, because the mechanism under study, complementary
error profiles across distinct parametric priors, requires lineage
diversity by construction, and homogeneous or persona-only
diversification demonstrably reproduces the epistemic-bubble failure
mode
(Sections [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")–[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Judicial Panel: Reliability and Negativity Bias ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).
Second, no specific model is *required*: the framework is
model-agnostic, and the configuration reported here is one instantiation
selected under a realistic academic research budget (affordable
OpenRouter/OpenAI endpoints); researchers with different access profiles
can substitute alternatives role-for-role.

| Role | Model | Selection rationale |
|----|----|----|
| Plaintiff Counsel | GPT-5-mini | Strong instruction-following under advocacy constraints |
| Defense Counsel | DeepSeek-V3.2 | Distinct pretraining lineage from Plaintiff |
| The Court | Qwen3-235B | Reliable query refinement and procedural control |
| Judge 1 | DeepSeek-R1 | Analytical rigor (deep CoT tracing) |
| Judge 2 | Hermes-3-405B | Distinct reasoning style; diversity of adjudication |
| Judge 3 | Qwen3-235B | Balanced abstention behaviour |

Table 9: Functional rationale for the heterogeneous role–model
assignment. Counsels operate at $`T{=}0.5`$ for argumentative diversity;
judges at $`T{=}0.3`$ for deterministic adjudication (validated in
Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Judicial Panel: Reliability and Negativity Bias ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

#### B.1.4 Hyperparameters

The novelty threshold $`\tau`$ was selected via grid search over
$`\{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30\}`$ on a held-out development subset of 20

|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Hyperparameter                  | Value                                |
| Max debate rounds               | 10                                   |
| Initial retrieval top-$`k`$     | 5                                    |
| Per-round retrieval top-$`k`$   | 3                                    |
| Novelty threshold               | 0.20                                 |
| Admissibility floor             | $`>`$0.5 admitted, $`>`$0.1 disputed |

### B.2 Expert Elicitation of Self-Reflection Weights

The self-reflection dimension weights in
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3.5 Self-Reflection and Critic Evaluation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
($`0.4`$ logic / $`0.3`$ novelty / $`0.3`$ rebuttal) were determined *a
priori* through a structured expert elicitation rather than post-hoc
tuning, following the SHELF framework ([O’Hagan et al.,
2006](#bib.bib55)) with a Delphi consensus protocol ([Brown,
1968](#bib.bib56)), a well-established methodology for systematically
eliciting and aggregating expert judgments under uncertainty.

Protocol. Seven independent experts spanning three competency areas
(legal reasoning, AI/LLM systems, and fact-checking) were presented with
a random sample of debate transcripts from development runs and asked to
assess the relative importance of logical coherence, evidence novelty,
and rebuttal engagement in determining argument quality, over two
anonymized Delphi rounds with controlled feedback.

Outcome. Expert consensus was strong (Kendall’s $`W=0.89`$,
$`p<0.005`$). Logic received the highest weight (0.4) as the
non-negotiable requirement for inferential validity; novelty and
rebuttal were weighted equally (0.3 each) to balance evidence discovery
against adversarial engagement without either dominating. The elicited
weights subsequently proved Pareto-efficient in operation: removing the
resulting reflection-driven stopping rule increases token usage by 17%
and debate rounds by 29% while changing accuracy by only 0.8 pp
(Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

### B.3 P-RAG Query Construction

To address the challenge of merging heterogeneous sources into a
coherent search strategy, P-RAG does not issue multiple separate
queries. Instead, it concatenates the three sources into a single
directed prompt, formulates an initial query via a lightweight LLM, and
passes it to the presiding Judge for rigorous refinement. This
guarantees a single, highly targeted natural-language query is executed
against the vector corpus per agent, per round.

#### Step 1: Gap Proposal (Counsel)

Each counsel identifies a discovery need from the current debate state:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

As {job_title}, analyze the current proceedings and identify a critical
gap in the available exhibits. What specific evidence do you need to
request to strengthen your case or challenge the

opposition?

Context: {debate_context}

% Last 4 transcript entries

Propose exactly one specific evidence need (1 sentence):

Concatenation of Sources: The agent’s newly identified evidential gap
(Source 2) and any unresolved discovery_need generated during the prior
round’s self-reflection (Source 3) are concatenated into a single
agent_request string:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,e2dhcF9wcm9wb3NhbH0uCkZvY3VzIGFsc28gb246IHtyZWZsZWN0aW9uX2Rpc2NvdmVyeV9uZWVkfQ==)

{gap_proposal}.

Focus also on: {reflection_discovery_need}

This combined agent_request is then injected alongside the last four
messages of the debate history (debate_context, Source 1) into the
formulation prompt below.

#### Step 2: Query Formulation (P-RAG Engine)

The combined discovery prompt is passed to the P-RAG LLM:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Based on the following proceedings context and legal request, formulate
a precise search query to retrieve relevant exhibits and evidence.

Debate Context: {debate_context}

Agent Request: {agent_request}

Generate a concise search query (1--2 sentences) that will retrieve the
most relevant evidence

#### Step 3: Judicial Query Refinement (The Court)

Before retrieval executes, the formulated query is reviewed and refined
by the presiding judge (The Court, Qwen3-235B-A22B):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

As the Court, you must maintain the quality and focus of evidence
discovery. A counsel has proposed the following search query:

Proposed Query: "{original_query}"

Context of proceedings: {debate_context}

Refine this query to be more precise, narrow the scope if necessary, and
ensure it follows scientific rigor. Respond ONLY with the refined query
string.

#### Novelty Scoring and Stopping Criteria

Retrieval applies the refined query to the FAISS index (all-MiniLM-L6-v2
embeddings). Each retrieved document $`d`$ receives a novelty score:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{novelty}(d)=1-\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\cos(e_{d},\,e_{p})
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$ is the current evidence pool. Documents with
novelty \< 0.2 are rejected. The retrieval terminates early if any of
the following criteria are met: (i) redundancy ratio $`>0.70`$, (ii)
relevance gain $`<0.05`$ vs. the previous round, or (iii) round counter
$`\geq 10`$.

### B.4 Embedding Normalization and Similarity Computation

For embedding-based similarity computation used in the evidence
retrieval. Each claim $`q`$ and abstract chunk $`d`$ is mapped to a
384-dimensional vector $`\mathbf{v}`$ using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2
bi-encoder from the sentence-transformers framework ([Reimers and
Gurevych, 2019](#bib.bib39)). To ensure that similarity depends only on
semantic orientation, raw embeddings are L2-normalized:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{\hat{v}}=\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}}=\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{384}v_{i}^{2}}}.
``` |  | (7) |

The similarity between a query embedding $`\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{q}`$ and a
chunk embedding $`\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{d}`$ is computed as their inner
product, which is equivalent to cosine similarity for unit vectors:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{sim}(q,d)=\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{q}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{d}=\cos(\theta).
``` |  | (8) |

The most semantically similar chunks are selected as the seed evidence
pool, with source journal and publication year preserved for provenance
context in subsequent deliberation.

### B.5 Pseudo-code

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ B.5 Pseudo-code ‣ Appendix B Implementation and Reproducibility Details ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
summarizes the workflow of PROClaim.

1: claim $`c`$, PubMed FAISS index $`\mathcal{D}`$, LLM agents
$`\{\text{Proponent},\text{Opponent},\text{Judge},\text{Critic}\}`$

2: final verdict
$`v\in\{\text{SUPPORT},\text{REFUTE},\text{INCONCLUSIVE}\}`$

3: Mine atomic premises $`\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\}`$ using
Argument Miner

4: Retrieve initial evidence
$`E_{0}\leftarrow\textsc{Retrieve}(c,\mathcal{D})`$

5: Evidence Negotiation & Arbitration

6: $`E_{0}\leftarrow`$ premise-grounded retrieval using $`\mathcal{P}`$

7: $`E_{0}\leftarrow`$ stance-conditioned retrieval for supporting and
refuting evidence

8: $`E_{0}\leftarrow`$ LLM admissibility scoring (Relevance $`\times`$
Credibility)

9: Initialize debate state $`S_{0}\leftarrow(\mathcal{P},E_{0})`$

10: for round $`t=1`$ to $`T`$ do

11:   $`E_{t}\leftarrow\textsc{P-RAG}(\mathcal{P},S_{t-1},\mathcal{D})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Progressive novelty-filtered retrieval

12:   Proponent generates argument $`a_{t}^{+}`$ from $`E_{t}`$

13:   Opponent generates counterargument $`a_{t}^{-}`$ from $`E_{t}`$

14:   Call Expert Witness to produce testimony $`\tau_{t}`$

15:   Compute self-reflection scores $`r_{t}^{+},r_{t}^{-}`$

16:   Critic evaluates arguments and updates debate state

17:
  $`S_{t}\leftarrow\textsc{UpdateState}(S_{t-1},a_{t}^{+},a_{t}^{-},\tau_{t})`$

18:   if evidence novelty $`<\epsilon`$ or debate converged or $`t=T`$
then

19:    break

20:   end if

21: end for

22: Swap roles of Proponent and Opponent

23: Re-run debate with swapped roles to obtain consistency record
$`S^{\mathrm{swap}}`$

24: Send debate records $`\{S_{T},S^{\mathrm{swap}}\}`$ to judicial
panel $`\{J_{1},J_{2},J_{3}\}`$

25: for each judge $`J_{i}`$ do

26:   $`v_{i}\leftarrow J_{i}(c,S_{T},S^{\mathrm{swap}})`$

27: end for

28: $`v\leftarrow\textsc{MajorityVote}(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3})`$

29: return $`v`$

Algorithm 1 One claim evaluation cycle of the P-RAG multi-agent debate
framework.

## Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics

### C.1 The ‘Burden of Refutation’ Standard

The framework’s structural decision to formally classify ‘Inconclusive‘
judicial panel verdicts as ‘SUPPORT‘ is derived directly from the
foundational legal concept of the burden of proof, which functions
analogously to the presumption of innocence (“innocent until proven
guilty”).

In a traditional courtroom, a defending party does not need to
absolutely guarantee their innocence to survive a trial; rather, the
prosecution bears the strict burden of definitively proving guilt. If
the prosecution’s evidence is ambiguous, controversial, or broadly
insufficient, the presiding jury is legally obligated to return a “Not
Guilty” verdict, even if they remain partially unsure.

Our multi-agent debate architecture mirrors this exact decision-making
protocol. When verifying controversial claims, the refuting agent
mathematically functions as the prosecution. If the refuting agent fails
to successfully furnish enough concrete, high-quality evidence to
convince the judicial panel to issue a definitive ‘Refute‘ consensus,
the panel will naturally return an ‘Inconclusive‘ stance. Under the
burden of proof, this ‘Inconclusive‘ ruling means the prosecution
completely failed to meet its evidentiary threshold. Consequently, the
original claim legally and logically survives the adversarial trial,
defaulting to ‘SUPPORT.‘

This standard is a core necessity of the framework’s design. It actively
prevents the multi-agent system from stalling on highly ambiguous cases
and faithfully operationalizes the adversarial mechanics utilized to
evaluate the Check-COVID dataset.

#### Sensitivity Analysis of the Verdict Mapping

Of the 120 majority-voted claims, 7.5% ($`\approx`$9 claims) receive an
Inconclusive verdict prior to mapping. To verify that the reported
performance is not an artifact of the mapping policy, we evaluate three
conditions
(Table [11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Sensitivity Analysis of the Verdict Mapping ‣ C.1 The ‘Burden of Refutation’ Standard ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")).

| Mapping Policy                        | Accuracy | Macro F1 |
|---------------------------------------|----------|----------|
| Inconclusive $`\to`$ Supported (ours) | 81.7%    | 0.817    |
| Inconclusive $`\to`$ Refuted          | 80.8%    | 0.808    |
| Inconclusive excluded                 | 83.8%    | 0.838    |

Table 11: Verdict-mapping sensitivity on Check-COVID (120 majority-voted
claims).

The 0.8 pp gap between the two mapping policies confirms that reported
performance is insensitive to this design choice; selection between them
is therefore correctly decided by theoretical grounding (the
Burden-of-Refutation principle above) rather than empirical convenience.
The excluded condition (83.8%) further validates that the panel’s
uncertainty signal is calibrated and meaningful: when the judicial panel
reaches a confident verdict, accuracy rises by 2.1 pp, confirming that
Inconclusive verdicts arise on genuinely harder claims rather than
serving as an accuracy-inflating abstention mechanism. Because excluding
abstentions is not a valid protocol for deployment scenarios that
require a verdict on every claim, we report the full-coverage number
(81.7%) as the primary metric throughout. Finally, the mapping is a
configurable parameter: sensitive medical or safety-critical deployments
should invert it (Inconclusive $`\to`$ Refuted) or route abstentions to
human review, as discussed in
§[Limitations](#Sx1 "Limitations ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification").

### C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details

#### C.2.1 Confidence Calibration Analysis

To ensure that the confidence scores produced by PROClaim reflect
empirical accuracy, we performed a post-hoc calibration of the consensus
weighting parameter ($`W_{\text{consensus}}`$). The calibration aims to
minimize the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{|B_{m}|}{N}\left|\text{acc}(B_{m})-\text{conf}(B_{m})\right|,
``` |  | (9) |

where $`N`$ is the total number of samples, $`B_{m}`$ is a bin of
predictions within a specific confidence range, and
$`\text{acc}(B_{m})`$ and $`\text{conf}(B_{m})`$ are the observed
accuracy and mean confidence of that bin, respectively.

Methodology
We conducted an exhaustive grid search over
$`W_{\text{consensus}}\in[0.5,0.9]`$ with a step size of $`0.1`$. To
prevent test-set leakage, the optimal weights were determined via 5-fold
cross-validation across the experimental metadata. The values for
$`c_{\text{base}}`$ were then adjusted by the secondary refinements
($`\delta_{\text{rs}}`$ and $`\delta_{\text{ref}}`$).

Results
Table
[12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ C.2.1 Confidence Calibration Analysis ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification")
summarizes the comparison between the baseline equal-weighting variant
($`W=0.6`$) and our final calibrated model ($`W=0.8`$). The $`0.8`$
weighting achieved a near-optimal ECE of $`0.0340`$, representing a
significant reduction in over-confidence compared to the experimental
variant.

| Variant                              | N   | Accuracy | ECE    |
|--------------------------------------|-----|----------|--------|
| $`W_{\text{consensus}}=0.6`$         | 118 | 95.76%   | 0.1802 |
| $`W_{\text{consensus}}=0.8`$ (Final) | 118 | 95.76%   | 0.0340 |

Table 12: Impact of Consensus Weighting on Calibration Error.

The bucket analysis for the final model (Table
[13](#A3.T13 "Table 13 ‣ C.2.1 Confidence Calibration Analysis ‣ C.2 Confidence Score: Calibration and Adjustment Details ‣ Appendix C Verdict and Confidence Mechanics ‣ Courtroom-Style Multi-Agent Debate with Progressive RAG and Role-Switching for Controversial Claim Verification"))
shows that the generated confidence scores closely align with observed
accuracy, particularly in the high-certainty bins where the system’s
majority-vote consensus is strongest. Calibration was performed on the
confidence-annotated development subset used for weight selection
($`N=118`$ claims with valid confidence scores), which is distinct from
the 120-claim majority-vote test evaluation reporting 81.7%. The
accuracy on this calibration subset is therefore not directly comparable
to the headline test accuracy; only the ECE reduction
($`0.18\to 0.034`$) is the relevant calibration outcome.

| Confidence Bin | N   | Observed Acc. | Mean Conf. |
|----------------|-----|---------------|------------|
| $`[0.6,0.7)`$  | 4   | 75.00%        | 0.6685     |
| $`[0.7,0.8)`$  | 4   | 100.00%       | 0.7365     |
| $`[0.8,0.9)`$  | 20  | 95.00%        | 0.8639     |
